If you are meeting `plant` for the first time, start here. This page gives you
the mental model — what the model tracks, how the pieces fit together, and where
each idea shows up in the code — without any equations. When you want the maths,
the [gentle maths primer](maths-primer.qmd) builds up the equations one step at a
time, and the [size-structured PDE](size-structured-pde.qmd) page has the full
treatment.

## What `plant` models

`plant` is a simulator for **forests of competing plants**. Given a set of plant
*strategies* (ways of being a plant — cheap fast-growing leaves, dense slow wood,
and so on), it works out how a patch of ground fills with vegetation over time,
how those plants shade and out-compete one another, and which strategies can
persist in the long run.

The trick is that it builds everything **from the bottom up**. Nothing about the
forest is assumed in advance: stand structure, size distributions, and
coexistence all *emerge* from the growth, death, and seeding of individual
plants.

## Three nested scales

The model is organised as three scales nested inside one another. Each scale is
built out of the one below it.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  subgraph M["🌍 Metacommunity — patches of every age, linked by dispersing seeds"]
    subgraph P["🌳 Patch — competing individuals sharing one light environment"]
      I["🌱 Individual — grows, dies, sets seed"]
    end
  end
```

- **Individual** — a single plant with a set of traits and a size (its height).
  It takes in light, grows, risks dying, and produces seeds.
- **Patch** — a small area of ground where many individuals grow together. They
  compete by shading one another, so every plant in the patch shares one common
  **light environment**. A disturbance (fire, storm, landslide…) can wipe a patch
  clean and reset it to bare ground.
- **Metacommunity** — the whole landscape: a large collection of patches, each at
  a different age since its last disturbance, all connected because seeds
  disperse freely between them.

A key simplification makes this tractable: because seeds mix across the whole
landscape, **one patch followed through its entire life stands in for the whole
metacommunity**. Simulating a single patch from bare ground to old age, and
knowing how common patches of each age are, is enough to describe everything.

## Two halves: biology and bookkeeping

Internally, `plant` separates cleanly into two parts.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  subgraph S["Strategy — the biology"]
    direction TB
    s1["a plant's size<br/>+ its light environment"] --> s2["growth, death,<br/>seed rates"]
  end
  subgraph D["Demographic core — the bookkeeping"]
    direction TB
    d1["rates, tracked<br/>over time"] --> d2["how the whole<br/>population changes"]
  end
  S -->|"rates plug in"| D
  models["FF16 · K93 · TF24"] -.->|"pick one"| S
```

- The **strategy** is the biology. Given a plant's size and the light it
  experiences, it returns three instantaneous rates: how fast the plant grows,
  how likely it is to die, and how many seeds it makes. This is where the
  photosynthesis, carbon budgets, and hydraulics live. `plant` ships with three
  strategies — [FF16](models/ff16.qmd), [K93](models/k93.qmd), and
  [TF24](models/tf24.qmd) — and you can [write your own](../contributing/implementing-a-strategy.qmd).
- The **demographic core** is the bookkeeping. It knows nothing about
  photosynthesis; it just takes those rates and integrates them over time to work
  out how a population of plants grows, thins, and reproduces. Swap the strategy
  and you swap the biology; the bookkeeping stays the same.

This split is why the [theory](index.qmd) is organised into *Core* (the
bookkeeping, shared by everything) and *Models* (the strategies).

## What the model actually tracks

Inside a patch, `plant` does not follow every individual plant separately.
Instead it tracks a **size distribution**: how many plants of each height are
present in the patch at a given age. Early on the distribution is a crowd of tiny
seedlings; as the patch ages it spreads out, thins, and a few tall winners pull
ahead.

The clever part is *how* it follows that distribution. Rather than chopping
height into fixed bins, `plant` tracks a handful of **cohorts** — groups of
plants that germinated at the same moment — and lets each one ride its own growth
trajectory upward. Each cohort is a moving point on the height axis, carrying a
"how many plants are here" density with it. This is the *characteristic method*,
and it is what makes the model both accurate and fast. (The
[characteristic method](implementation/characteristic-method.qmd) and
[node-spacing](implementation/node-spacing.qmd) pages cover the machinery.)

## Competition is a feedback loop

Everything interesting in `plant` comes from one feedback loop. Plants deploy
leaf area; leaf area casts shade; shade changes the light every plant
experiences; and that light feeds straight back into how fast each plant grows
and how likely it is to survive.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["Plants deploy<br/>leaf area"] --> B["Canopy casts shade —<br/>the light environment"]
  B --> C["Less light below<br/>slows growth,<br/>raises mortality"]
  C --> D["Size distribution<br/>shifts: some win,<br/>some die"]
  D --> A
```

This loop is what produces **self-thinning** (crowded stands lose stems as they
grow), **succession** (the mix of winners changes over time), and the vertical
canopy structure of a real forest — none of it built in by hand.

## Paying for itself: the birth-rate loop

There is one more loop, at the landscape scale. Seeds produced in patches
disperse across the whole metacommunity and rain back down to start new plants.
For the metacommunity to be at equilibrium, a strategy must **pay for itself**:
the seeds it exports over a patch's lifetime must match the seeds arriving to
sustain it.

`plant` finds that balance by solving a fixed point — guessing a seed-arrival
rate, running a patch to see how many seeds come back out, and adjusting until
the two agree.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["Guess a seed-<br/>arrival rate"] --> B["Run one patch<br/>through its whole life"]
  B --> C["Count the seeds<br/>it exports"]
  C --> Q{"exported =<br/>assumed?"}
  Q -->|"no"| E["Adjust the rate"]
  E --> B
  Q -->|"yes"| F["Equilibrium —<br/>the strategy<br/>pays for itself"]
```

This is exactly what happens when you call `run_scm(..., refine_schedule = TRUE)`
in the guides. Once you can find that self-consistent birth rate, you can ask the
deeper question `plant` was built for: *which strategies can invade, coexist, or
win?* — the subject of the [adaptive dynamics](adaptive-dynamics.qmd) page.

## From idea to code

Each concept above has a direct counterpart in the package:

| Idea | In `plant` | Guide |
|------|-----------|-------|
| Pick a strategy & its biology | `scm_base_parameters("FF16")`, `add_strategies()` | [Strategies & traits](../guides/strategies.qmd) |
| Set the light / rainfall environment | `Environment()` | [Extrinsic drivers](../guides/extrinsic-drivers.qmd) |
| Grow a single plant | `FF16_Individual()` | [Your first individual](../guides/first-individual.qmd) |
| Run a patch through its life | `run_scm()` | [Patch dynamics](../guides/patch-dynamics.qmd) |
| Find the birth rate that balances | `run_scm(..., refine_schedule = TRUE)` | [Self-thinning](../guides/self-thinning.qmd) |
| Tidy & expand the outputs | `collect = TRUE`, `expand_state()` | [Example analysis](../guides/example-analysis.qmd) |
